sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Inspection evaluates (i) conformance of components to material specifications, (ii) conformance of construction methods to execution specifications, (iii) site or soil conditions needing changes to installation or design, (iv) short-term performance (load testing) and (v) long-term monitoring if contracted. Short-term monitoring (wall deflection, ground movement, nail load tests) is by the Owner or Contractor; long-term monitoring is usually by the Owner. The inspector keeps installation logs, a daily log and a field book.
sections.body: 9.1 Introduction (pp. 231-232). The chapter covers the most common aspects of soil nail wall inspection and monitoring, whatever the contracting approach and whoever is assigned inspection; additional measures may be needed for a given project. Inspection evaluates: (i) conformance of system components to material specifications; (ii) conformance of construction methods to execution specifications, if any; (iii) identification of site or soil conditions that require adjustment to the installation procedures or to the original design; (iv) conformance to short-term performance specifications (load testing); and (v) long-term monitoring, if required by contract. A valuable source is the Soil Nailing Field Inspector's Manual (Porterfield et al. 1994). Short-term monitoring is usually limited to measurements during and possibly shortly after construction and may include vertical and lateral wall deflection, ground movement near the wall and load testing of soil nails; long-term monitoring is less typical and usually continues the short-term measurements. Short-term monitoring can be by the Owner or the Contractor depending on the contracting approach; long-term monitoring is usually by the Owner. The inspection personnel ensure all required construction activities and testing are completed per the contract; the inspector must understand soil nail wall construction, be intimately familiar with the design drawings and specifications, carry the necessary safety gear and instruments (checking any Contractor-provided gear works), and keep soil nail installation logs, a daily log and field book.
key_points: Inspection: material conformance, method conformance, changed site or soil conditions, load testing, long-term monitoring
Applies whatever the contracting approach and whoever performs inspection
Reference: Soil Nailing Field Inspector's Manual (Porterfield et al. 1994)
Short-term monitoring: wall deflection, nearby ground movement, nail load tests; by Owner or Contractor
Long-term monitoring less typical, usually by the Owner
Inspector keeps soil nail installation logs, a daily log and a field book
sections.applicability: Scope and responsibilities of soil nail wall construction inspection and monitoring.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Materials
sections.summary: Inspection of construction materials: acceptance by inspection, certification and testing (9.2.1), storage (9.2.2) and inspection of tendon corrosion protection (9.2.3).
sections.body: 9.2 Inspection of Construction Materials (pp. 232-233). Subsections 9.2.1 Materials Inspection to 9.2.3 Inspection of Corrosion Protection.
key_points: Materials are accepted, stored and checked for corrosion protection damage before use
sections.applicability: Acceptance, storage and corrosion-protection inspection of soil nail materials.

subsections.title: Materials Inspection
subsections.summary: Material quality is controlled by visual examination, manufacturer or supplier certification, and laboratory testing of samples. Steel components (tendons, plates, nuts, washers, WWM, rebar) are accepted on mill certifications; cement on the producer's certification pending grout compressive tests and observation of installation; centralizers, coatings, additives, sheathing, drainage material and piping on manufacturers' certificates, always with a visual check for damage. Potable water is generally suitable for grout or shotcrete without testing.
subsections.body: 9.2.1 Materials Inspection (p. 232). The quality of all materials is controlled by one or a combination of: visual examination for defects due to poor workmanship, contamination or handling damage; certification by the manufacturer or supplier that the materials comply with the design and specifications; and laboratory testing of representative samples delivered to the site or approved storage area. Steel components such as tendons, bearing plates, nuts, washers, welded wire mesh (WWM) and reinforcing bars are normally accepted based on mill certifications. Cement is accepted on the cement producer's certification pending the results of unconfined compressive testing on grout and observation of soil nail installation. Centralizers, coatings, grout additives, sheathing, geocomposite drainage material and piping are normally accepted on manufacturers' certificates. In addition, visual inspection is necessary to establish whether materials were damaged in transport or storage. Water for grout or shotcrete must be free from chemical or organic material that may affect performance; potable water is generally suitable without testing.
key_points: Quality control by visual examination, certification and laboratory testing
Steel components accepted on mill certifications
Cement accepted on the producer's certification pending grout compression tests
Other materials on manufacturers' certificates, plus a visual check for transport or storage damage
Potable water generally suitable for grout or shotcrete without testing
subsections.applicability: Acceptance of soil nail wall construction materials.

subsections.title: Storage
subsections.summary: Inspection verifies proper storage: materials kept in suitable locations and protected from the elements and construction; cement (bagged or bulk) dry and off the ground, bags not stacked too high; tendons on supports off the ground and its moisture, spaced to prevent excessive bending that could compromise tolerances or cover; other steel and drainage materials in suitable containers.
subsections.body: 9.2.2 Storage (pp. 232-233). Inspection must verify proper storage of the materials that will form part of the wall: all materials kept in a suitable location and protected against deterioration by the elements and construction activities. Cement, supplied bagged or in bulk, must be kept dry and elevated from the ground; the Contractor should avoid stacking bags too high, to prevent over compaction of the cement. Tendons must be placed on supports to prevent contact with the ground and its moisture, with supports spaced to prevent excessive bending, which may compromise the tolerances or the minimum cover. Other steel components and drainage materials should be stored in suitable containers and protected from damage.
key_points: Materials protected from the elements and construction activities
Cement dry and off the ground; bags not stacked too high
Tendons on supports spaced to prevent excessive bending
subsections.applicability: Storage of soil nail materials on site.

subsections.title: Inspection of Corrosion Protection
subsections.summary: Corrosion protection of every tendon is inspected on site before acceptance; damaged tendons are repaired if possible or replaced. Encapsulation: check for cracks or scores (repairs per the manufacturer, approved by the Owner) and tap a representative number for voids, replacing tendons with voids. Epoxy: check for damage, bare steel and color variation; nicks repaired with the manufacturer's kit, but bare areas or thickness outside the Chapter 7 range mean replacement. Galvanized tendons are inspected similarly.
subsections.body: 9.2.3 Inspection of Corrosion Protection (p. 233). The corrosion protection of all tendons must be inspected at the project site before acceptance and use; tendons with damaged protection must be repaired, if possible, or replaced, and other protected steel elements inspected likewise. Encapsulated tendons are usually delivered assembled, with the annulus between sheath and tendon grouted at the production facility; inspection includes visual examination for surface damage such as cracks or scores, which may be repaired by procedures approved by the manufacturer and subject to the Owner's approval. A representative number should be checked for voids by lightly tapping the encapsulation with a steel rod and listening for hollow sounds; tendons with voids should generally be replaced rather than repaired. Epoxy-coated tendons are susceptible to impact and scarring: equipment should not travel on them and they should not be dragged, excessively bent or field cut. Tendons are occasionally incompletely coated at the factory, with bare steel or significant color variations; the coating should be visually examined, nicks and dents may be repaired with the manufacturer's kit, but tendons with bare steel or coating thickness outside the Chapter 7 range should be replaced. Galvanized tendons are inspected by similar procedures, well supported in lifting and handling, and repairs of limited damage must strictly follow the manufacturer's recommendations.
key_points: Every tendon's corrosion protection inspected on site before acceptance
Encapsulation: check for cracks or scores; tap for voids; replace tendons with voids
Epoxy: repair nicks with the manufacturer's kit; replace bare steel or out-of-range thickness (Chapter 7)
Galvanized tendons: inspected like epoxy; repairs per the manufacturer
subsections.applicability: Site inspection of soil nail corrosion protection.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Activities
sections.summary: Inspection of construction activities: who inspects (9.3.1), excavation (9.3.2), drilling (9.3.3), tendon installation (9.3.4), grouting (9.3.5), geocomposite strip drains (9.3.6) and wall facing (9.3.7), with the items the inspector reports for each.
sections.body: 9.3 Inspection of Construction Activities (pp. 233-241). Subsections 9.3.1 Introduction to 9.3.7 Wall Facing.
key_points: Inspection items for each major construction step
sections.applicability: Organization of construction inspection and inspection of soil nail wall excavation.

subsections.title: Introduction
subsections.summary: Construction inspection is by qualified individuals: the Geotechnical Engineer, the wall Designer or Specialty Contractor, a third party, or a combination; 'inspector' means whoever inspects a given item. A third-party firm may not be qualified for some specialized tasks, which then go to the geotechnical engineer or wall designer; the Owner or designer sets who does what. Porterfield et al. (1994) give more detail on inspection methods, testing, forms and difficult ground.
subsections.body: 9.3.1 Introduction (pp. 233-234). Inspection during construction should be carried out by qualified individuals; depending on the project it may be done by the Geotechnical Engineer, the wall Designer or Specialty Contractor, a third party, or a combination. In this chapter 'inspector' refers to the person or entity inspecting a given item. A third-party inspection firm may not be qualified for certain specialized tasks; the geotechnical engineer or the wall designer must then be engaged to complete them. The chapter does not differentiate between inspection entities and focuses on the necessary tasks; the differentiation must be established by the Owner or the wall designer as needed. Porterfield et al. (1994) give considerably greater detail on inspection methods, nail testing, inspection forms and handling difficult ground during construction.
key_points: Inspection by qualified individuals: geotechnical engineer, designer, specialty contractor or third party
Specialized tasks a third party cannot do go to the geotechnical engineer or wall designer
Porterfield et al. (1994): more detail on methods, testing, forms and difficult ground
subsections.applicability: Who inspects soil nail wall construction.

subsections.title: Excavation
subsections.summary: Excavation is mass excavation (access and grading) or bench excavation to the neat line. The inspector verifies mass excavation does not encroach on the partly built wall and the neat line and grade are within tolerance, and reports: excavated and face materials and moisture (with sketches); unexpected soft zones, seepage or fill, for the designer; recurrent raveling or sloughing; the face condition at the start and end of each day (generally not left unprotected overnight); and the stability of the retained ground at least twice a day, out to about one wall height.
subsections.body: 9.3.2 Excavation (pp. 234-235). Two types of excavation generally occur: (1) mass excavation for equipment access and general site grading; and (2) bench excavations for the wall, to the finished wall line on the plans ('neat line'). During mass excavation the inspector must verify that the excavation does not encroach on the partially completed wall, because uncontrolled excavation nearby could affect its stability. The Contractor completes the excavation to neat line and grade and the inspector verifies compliance within tolerance. The inspector reports: the type, nature and moisture of excavated materials and of the face (moisture and seepage, soft zones, sloughing and overbreaks, boulders, manmade features or obstructions, with dimensioned sketches located in plan and elevation); unexpected soft zones, seepage areas or fill, reported to the Owner's or Contractor's designer (seepage may need extra drainage; soft soil or fill not considered in design may be serious and warrant a design revision); recurrent raveling or sloughing of the face, reported to the Owner as it may cause excessive ground movement and harm performance, with the Contractor addressing overbreaks, sloughing and protruding cobbles or boulders; the condition of the face at the start and end of each work day and any portions left unprotected (generally, but not always, the face should not be left unprotected overnight); and the stability of the retained soils, the area behind or upslope of the wall and the excavation bottom, at least twice a day, examining (if safe) the ground surface for cracks, openings, movement or seepage and watching utilities, manholes and pavements, with conditions noted on the first day as a baseline. Ground movements may occur behind the wall to a distance equal to the wall height; inspection beyond is usually unnecessary; visual inspection may be adjusted to the instrumentation and monitoring.
key_points: Mass excavation must not encroach on the partly built wall; bench excavation to the neat line within tolerance
Report materials, moisture, seepage, soft zones, overbreaks, boulders and obstructions with sketches
Unexpected soft zones, seepage or fill reported to the designer; may warrant a design revision
Face generally not left unprotected overnight
Check retained ground stability at least twice a day, to about one wall height behind the wall
Record ground, structure and utility conditions on the first day as a baseline
subsections.applicability: Inspection of soil nail wall excavation.

subsections.title: Drilling
subsections.summary: Drill holes located and oriented as on the plans within tolerance, deviations reported; the mast angle must represent the tendon inclination at the face. The inspector records the equipment and method, drill fluid (or HBSN grout) pressure, flow and volume (clogged return, connection to other holes, heave), subsidence or large soil removal, tools and casing, cuttings and drilling time, bit diameter and lengths, and how long the hole stays open (tendon inserted and grouted immediately in general). HBSNs: drilling rate and grout pressure, bit and grout ports, and returned cuttings.
subsections.body: 9.3.3 Drilling (pp. 235-237). The drill holes should be located and oriented as shown on the plans and within the specified tolerances; deviations beyond tolerance must be noted and communicated to the Owner. The drill mast angle is generally measured with an angle tool on the mast, taking care that it represents the tendon inclination as it enters the face. The inspector reports: the equipment and installation method (understanding the Contractor's drilling systems, Chapter 3, and their effects on the borehole and ground); the pressure, flow rate and volume of drill fluid (or grout for HBSNs), noting clogged return flush, connection with other holes or the ground surface, or heave from pressurization; subsidence above the drilling location or large soil removal with little advancement, which require modified procedures; the drilling method and tools (bit type, casing diameter and final length, drill string length, drilling fluid), the cuttings and material drilled, fluid loss, zones of difficult and easy drilling, and the effective drilling time, which helps discern material changes within the site though it cannot be correlated with ground properties; the lengths of bit, drill string and casing before drilling and the final hole length after flushing and before tendon insertion, and the bit diameter, which should equal the nominal hole diameter; and the time the hole is left open, which should be short in soil to limit seepage, caving or degradation; in general a tendon is inserted and grouted immediately after drilling, with exceptions set per project if the hole is flushed as needed. For hollow bars, the inspector records: the drilling rate and grout pressure at the surface with consistent grout return to the face (cuttings are very hard to see in grout flush); the drill bit type and the number and size of grout exit ports, usually once per project unless changed; and the type of returned soil cuttings, occasionally sieve-washing the outflow grout, useful in widely varying grain sizes or organic soils.
key_points: Holes located and oriented within tolerance; deviations reported to the Owner
Mast angle must represent the tendon inclination at the face
Record drill fluid (or HBSN grout) pressure, flow and volume; clogged return, hole connection or heave
Record tools, casing, cuttings, fluid loss, difficult or easy drilling and effective drilling time
Bit diameter should equal the nominal drill hole diameter
Tendon generally inserted and grouted immediately after drilling
HBSNs: drilling rate and grout pressure, bit and grout ports, sieve-washed cuttings
subsections.applicability: Inspection of soil nail drilling, including hollow bar installation.

subsections.title: Tendon Installation
subsections.summary: The inspector verifies each tendon's length, diameter, steel grade, centralizers and corrosion protection; inability to insert it to the minimum length indicates caving or sloughing (the drilling log rules out short drilling). Tendons handled carefully and supported when lifted; centralizers stiff and large enough for the minimum grout cover, spaced as specified without impeding tremied grout (or, for HBSNs, drilling grout and cuttings).
subsections.body: 9.3.4 Tendon Installation (p. 237). The inspection personnel must verify that each tendon meets the length, diameter, steel grade, centralizer and corrosion protection requirements of the plans and specifications. The tendon must be inserted to the minimum specified length; inability to do so indicates an unacceptable condition caused by caving or sloughing of the hole, and insufficient drilled length can be ruled out from the drilling log kept by the inspector for each nail. Tendons must be handled carefully, with adequate support when lifted by drill rigs or cranes. Centralizers should be stiff and large enough to provide the minimum specified grout cover and spaced as shown on the drawings or specifications, without impeding the free flow of tremied grout or, for HBSNs, the drilling grout and flushed cuttings. The Contractor must use suitable handling and lifting devices to prevent damage to the corrosion protection.
key_points: Verify tendon length, diameter, grade, centralizers and corrosion protection
Inability to insert to the minimum length indicates caving or sloughing
Centralizers stiff and large enough for the minimum grout cover, not impeding grout flow
subsections.applicability: Inspection of soil nail tendon installation.

subsections.title: Grouting
subsections.summary: Grout must fill the whole nail without voids; the inspector verifies it indirectly from the hole inspection and grout volume. Tremie to the hole bottom, end kept below the grout surface; no reversed auger rotation on extraction. Injected volume at least theoretical, often 10 to 30 percent more; below 100 or above 130 percent, notify the Contractor and Owner. Specific gravity of fluid grout is the primary production QC, calibrated with cube tests (ASTM C109) at the start; target 1.8 to 1.9 for over 4,000 psi; HBSN drilling grout 1.4 to 1.6.
subsections.body: 9.3.5 Grouting (pp. 237-239). The entire length of the nail should be grouted without voids, soil intrusion or gaps; the inspector generally cannot verify this directly but does so indirectly by inspecting the drill hole before grouting (including its drilled length) and recording the injected grout volume. The inspector verifies that grout is injected by tremie pipe inserted to the bottom of the hole in a continuous process, the withdrawal rate keeping the pipe end always below the grout surface. Grouting may precede or follow tendon insertion; if after, the tendon volume is considered in the theoretical volume, and the tremie hose must be attached so as not to coil during insertion and to be pulled out without damaging the tendon or its protection; grouting can also be done within a temporary casing followed by nail insertion and casing extraction. With hollow-stem augers, the Contractor should not reverse the auger rotation during extraction, which mixes soil with the grout and reduces bond strength. The inspector records the grout volume (calibrated holding tank or flowmeter), from when final grout enters the hole until it exits free of impurities; it must be at least the theoretical hole volume and is often 10 to 30 percent larger; if less than 100 percent or greater than 130 percent of theoretical, the Contractor and the Owner must be notified and remedial measures undertaken if needed. Grout specific gravity and strength are measured: for production nails, the specific gravity of the newly prepared fluid grout should be the primary QC mechanism, preferred to compression tests, because in neat cement grout it relates directly to the water-cement ratio and hence strength. Grout cubes made with grout of known specific gravity and the project mixing equipment are tested at the start for each mix design to confirm the strength; additional comparison tests are made for long projects, many nails, or changes in cement, water, admixtures, batching or mixing equipment. Specific gravity is measured with an API balance (Baroid mud balance) per ASTM D4380 or API RP 13B (API 2009); the target is typically 1.8 to 1.9 for fluid, pumpable grout over the commonly used 4,000 psi; cubes are tested per ASTM C109; specifications set test type and minimum frequency. For HBSNs, drilling grout may be 1.4 to 1.6 and the final grout 1.8 to 1.9, the nail complete when the heavier grout returns to the face.
key_points: Grout integrity verified indirectly: hole inspection and grout volume
Tremie from the hole bottom, end kept below the grout surface; no reversed auger rotation
Grout volume at least theoretical, often 10-30 percent more; notify below 100 or above 130 percent
Fluid grout specific gravity is the primary production QC, calibrated by cube tests at the start
Target specific gravity 1.8 to 1.9 (over 4,000 psi); API balance per ASTM D4380 or API RP 13B; cubes per ASTM C109
HBSNs: drilling grout 1.4 to 1.6, final grout 1.8 to 1.9 until it returns to the face
subsections.applicability: Inspection of soil nail grouting and grout quality control.

subsections.title: Geocomposite Strip Drains
subsections.summary: After each lift's excavation and nail installation, geocomposite strip drains are placed vertically at the specified intervals, continuous from top to bottom, with any impermeable liner facing the shotcrete, not the soil. At the base they connect to a footing drain or to weep holes at the strip locations, with filter fabric behind the weep holes or around drainage aggregate. Footing drains: perforated pipe in drainage gravel, sloped as on the plans; the pipe is not wrapped in fabric, the aggregate may be.
subsections.body: 9.3.6 Geocomposite Strip Drains (p. 239). Once the final wall line excavation and nail installation are completed for each lift, the geocomposite strip drains are placed vertically at the specified intervals, continuous from the top to the bottom of the wall, as verified by the inspector against the drawings and specifications. Strip drains often have an impermeable protective liner on one side, which must not be placed against the soil but positioned to receive shotcrete. At the base, strip drains connect either to a footing drain below finished grade or to weep holes through the finished wall, located and spaced as on the plans to coincide with the strip drains; filter fabric is placed against the weep holes behind the wall to prevent clogging, or drainage aggregate, if used, is wrapped in filter fabric. Footing drains are perforated pipe embedded in drainage gravel, sloped along the wall alignment as shown; the perforated pipe should not be wrapped in filter fabric, but the surrounding aggregate may be.
key_points: Strip drains vertical at specified intervals, continuous top to bottom
Impermeable liner faces the shotcrete, not the soil
Base connection to a footing drain or weep holes at the strip locations, with filter fabric
Footing drain pipe not wrapped in fabric; the aggregate may be
subsections.applicability: Inspection of geocomposite strip drains and footing drains.

subsections.title: Wall Facing
subsections.summary: Reinforcement (WWM, rebar) placed to dimensions, locations and laps, then shotcrete; facing may precede drilling where standup time is poor. Cold joints cleaned with water and air or air; no heavy vibration nearby. A certified (ACI or ASA), pre-qualified nozzleman is most critical. Practice: nozzle perpendicular, 2 to 5 ft (wet-mix) or 3 to 6 ft (dry-mix), start at the bottom, no voids behind bars, plates or mesh, edges by screed boards or wires. Check thickness, finish, plates and studs set in wet shotcrete; CIP facing per concrete practice.
subsections.body: 9.3.7 Wall Facing (pp. 239-241). After the strip drains are installed, reinforcing steel is placed and shotcrete applied to the specified lines and grades; WWM and rebar must have the proper dimensions, locations and overlap. Where site conditions require (e.g., poor standup time) or by the Contractor's preference, the shotcrete facing may be placed before nails are drilled. Conventional shotcrete procedures in the specifications (Appendices E and F) apply; equipment causing excessive vibration should not operate near shotcreting, to reduce rebound (printed 'i.e., shotcrete slump'). The overlying cold joint must be cleaned before the underlying lift is shot, by injected water with compressed air or by compressed air, without eroding the soil face below. The most critical factor is an experienced nozzleman; specifications may require ACI or American Shotcrete Association (ASA) certification and a pre-qualification test panel. Recommended practice: nozzle perpendicular to the surface except when shooting around bars; nozzle distance 2 to 5 ft for wet-mix and 3 to 6 ft for dry-mix; placement starting at the bottom; no voids behind bars, plates or mesh; sharp edges and accurate lines set by screen boards, guide wires and/or depth spacers. The inspector checks the shotcrete lines and minimum thickness within tolerance, the surface finish and inclination, and that bearing plates with the required headed studs are set while the shotcrete is wet and without voids beneath (for an initial facing, the proper number and diameter of studs). A final cast-in-place facing follows typical CIP concrete inspection: reinforcement firmly placed to the specified locations and dimensions, concrete and shotcrete thicknesses as shown, and no deleterious material on the steel before pumping.
key_points: WWM and rebar placed to dimensions, locations and laps; facing may precede drilling where standup time is poor
Cold joints cleaned with water and air or air, without eroding the face below
Experienced nozzleman most critical; ACI or ASA certification and a test panel may be required
Nozzle perpendicular; 2 to 5 ft wet-mix, 3 to 6 ft dry-mix; start at the bottom; no voids behind steel
Bearing plates and headed studs set in wet shotcrete without voids beneath
Final CIP facing inspected as cast-in-place concrete
subsections.applicability: Inspection of shotcrete and cast-in-place soil nail wall facings.

sections.title: Load Testing
sections.summary: Load testing of soil nails: purpose, debonding and test types (9.4.1), equipment (9.4.2), verification tests with Eqs. 9.1-9.4 and Table 9.1 (9.4.3), proof tests with Eqs. 9.5-9.8 and Table 9.2 (9.4.4), creep criteria (9.4.5) and strain gauges (9.4.6).
sections.body: 9.4 Load Testing (pp. 241-258). Subsections 9.4.1 Introduction to 9.4.6 Strain Gauges.
key_points: Verification, proof and creep tests with their load schedules and acceptance criteria
sections.applicability: Purpose, types and selection of soil nail load tests.

subsections.title: Introduction
subsections.summary: Load tests verify that design loads are carried without excessive movement and with an adequate factor of safety, and check the Contractor's methods; each row is normally tested before the next lower level. Test nails have a bonded length in the target layer and an unbonded length above; grout above the bond length gives artificially high bond (the 'donut' effect). Verification tests (sacrificial; commonly two per major stratum) reach at least the nominal bond resistance; proof tests on at least 5 percent of production nails; creep tests hold 10 to 60 minutes.
subsections.body: 9.4.1 Introduction (pp. 241-243). Soil nails are load tested in the field to verify that the design loads can be carried without excessive movements and with an adequate factor of safety, and to verify the Contractor's drilling, installation and grouting before and during construction; changes in ground or procedures may require more testing. It is standard practice to complete testing in each row before progressing to the next lower level, which the Engineer may relax, most often for long walls. If results show faulty practices or insufficient resistance, the Contractor alters installation or construction methods; test procedures and acceptance criteria must be in the specifications. The inspector observes and logs the tests, ensures the schedule follows the specifications and approved submittals, and may help select proof test nails. Test nails need a bonded length in the layer where bond is measured and an unbonded length above (in proof tests, the minimum stressing length); the Contractor may debond by any method shown to be effective. Grout must not be pumped above the assumed bond length, since load would transfer up through grout in the unbonded zone (the 'donut' effect, Cadden et al. 2010) and give artificially high bond stresses. Typical methods mark the top of the bonded zone with a painted centralizer or survey ribbon before insertion; after testing and acceptance the unbonded length of all test nails is grouted. For HBSNs, grouted full length when drilled, the grout can be flushed out with a tremie and water, or a pre-installed smooth casing used as bond breaker, though Cadden et al. (2010) found the latter gave artificially high bond strengths; no accepted procedure exists, so contractors' reported bond strengths vary greatly. Verification Load Tests (9.4.1a, p. 242): verify that the pullout capacity from the Contractor's methods matches the design pullout capacity and bond strengths, to a maximum load inducing bond stresses at least equal to the nominal bond resistance for the stratum; an oversized tendon may be needed to reach pullout. The Engineer sets the number by ground and geometry, considering the strata to which production nails are bonded, commonly two tests in each anticipated major stratum, or by the design nail length; locations are shown in the project documents; more may be required after substantive changes in methods or ground variability. They are on sacrificial nails not part of the permanent work. Proof Tests (9.4.1b, p. 243): on a minimum of 5 percent of production nails during construction, to verify no significant variation along the wall, selected using installation records, e.g., where adjacent nails showed irregular drilling, low grout take or redrilling; verification tests do not count toward the 5 percent. Creep Tests (9.4.1c, p. 243): part of verification and proof testing, measuring movement at constant load with a sustained hold of 10 to 60 minutes, to ensure the nail carries the load through the service life with low or predictable creep.
key_points: Each row normally tested before excavating to the next lower level (may be relaxed by the Engineer)
Bonded length in the target layer, unbonded length above; debonding by any method shown effective
No grout above the bond length (the 'donut' effect gives artificially high bond; Cadden et al. 2010)
Unbonded length of test nails grouted after acceptance
HBSN debonding has no accepted procedure; reported bond strengths vary greatly
Verification tests: sacrificial nails, at least the nominal bond resistance, commonly two per major stratum
Proof tests on at least 5 percent of production nails; verification tests not counted
Creep tests: constant load held 10 to 60 minutes
subsections.applicability: Purpose and types of soil nail load tests.

subsections.title: Equipment for Testing
subsections.summary: A center-hole hydraulic jack and pump load the tendon, aligned with the nail, reacting on a sized jacking frame or block (not on the grout column); alignment load AL not over 2.5 percent of the maximum test load; test load not over 80 percent of the jack rating (Figures 9.1-9.3). One, preferably two, dial gauges on an independent support, within 5 degrees of the nail axis, zeroed after AL, reading to 0.001 in., travel at least the elastic elongation plus 1 in. or 2 in. A load cell may monitor creep holds; calibrations obtained before testing.
subsections.body: 9.4.2 Equipment for Testing (pp. 243-246). A center-hole hydraulic jack and pump apply the test load to the tendon, with the jack and nail axes aligned for uniform loading. A jacking frame or reaction block between the shotcrete or excavation face and the jack must be sized to avoid overstressing the bearing surface and should not react directly against the grout column. Once the jack is centered, an alignment load (AL), not exceeding 2.5 percent of the maximum test load, secures the equipment and removes slack. The jack must be sized so the anticipated test load is not greater than 80% of its rated capacity. Figures 9.1 and 9.2 show typical testing operations. Nail head movement is measured with at least one, preferably two, dial gauges on a tripod or rigid support independent of the jacking setup and wall; two give an average under slight eccentricity and a backup. Gauges are aligned within 5 degrees of the nail axis, zeroed after AL, read to the nearest 0.001 in., and accommodate a travel of at least the estimated elastic elongation at the maximum test load plus 1 in., or at least 2 in. A pressure gauge correlates jack pressure with load; at the Owner's discretion a center-hole load cell in series with the jack is used in creep tests, since in long holds a pressure gauge lacks the resolution to show small load loss while the pump is adjusted. Recent calibration data for jack, pressure gauge and load cell must be obtained from the Contractor before testing. Figure 9.3 shows a typical jack; its inclination-adjustable support is not necessary in typical practice (Figure 9.2).
key_points: Center-hole jack aligned with the nail; reaction frame sized and not bearing on the grout column
Alignment load AL not over 2.5 percent of the maximum test load
Test load not over 80 percent of the rated jack capacity
One, preferably two, dial gauges on an independent support, within 5 degrees, reading to 0.001 in.
Gauge travel at least the elastic elongation plus 1 in., or at least 2 in.
Load cell for creep holds at the Owner's discretion; calibrations before testing

subsections.title: Details of Verification Testing
subsections.summary: Verification tests on sacrificial nails, built as designed and by production methods, ideally to pullout; at least to the nominal bond strength. Unbonded length at least 3 ft in the hole plus jack and tail length; no fully grouted nails. LB VT max = At fy CRTY / rPO (Eq. 9.1, CRTY 0.9) or At fu CRTU / rPO (Eq. 9.2, CRTU 0.8); LB VT 10 ft to LB VT max, else a bigger tendon. VTL = LB VT rPO (Eq. 9.3), an ultimate load. Table 9.1 schedule, creep at 0.75 VTL for 60 min. Acceptance: no pullout below 1.00 VTL; movement over 0.8 VTL LUB/(E At) (Eq. 9.4); creep per 9.4.5.
subsections.body: 9.4.3 Details of Verification Testing (pp. 246-252). Verification tests are completed on non-production, sacrificial nails before construction, and may be required during production for different in situ conditions or installation methods; they are on nails as designed and built by the production methods. Ideally they reach pullout (the load at which further increments only produce continued movement) at the maximum test load, but pullout may occur earlier or not at all. They give the actual bond resistance if carried to pullout, verify that it exceeds the nominal bond resistance used in design, and show creep potential. At a minimum, loading must reach a load defined by the nominal bond strength; higher loads, preferably to pullout, give more information and may lead to more economical nails. Test nails must have a bonded (grouted) and an unbonded length; fully grouted nails must not be used. The unbonded length extends from the back of the bearing plate to the top of the bonded length and must be at least 3 ft within the hole, to avoid transferring stresses from under the plate to the upper bond zone; extra bar outside the hole (jack length and 'tail' length) connects the test assembly. The bonded length LB VT is chosen so a bond limit state is reached before a tensile one: (1) LB VT max = At x fy x CRTY / rPO for Grades 60 and 75 and other mild steel per ASTM A615 (Eq. 9.1), or At x fu x CRTU / rPO for Grade 150 and other high-strength steel per ASTM A722 (Eq. 9.2), with CRTY = 0.9, CRTU = 0.8, At the test tendon area, fy the yield and fu the ultimate tensile strength, and rPO = pi x qu x DDH; (2) if LB VT max > 10 ft, select 10 ft <= LB VT <= LB VT max; (3) if LB VT max < 10 (printed without unit), select LB VT = 10 ft and increase the tendon size until LB VT max > 10 ft. The Verification Test Load is VTL = LB VT x rPO (Eq. 9.3), a maximum 'ultimate' load, not a 'design' load as in the previous manual (where the maximum was 2.0 times the design load), so the Table 9.1 factors differ; VTL depends on no safety or resistance factor for pullout. Loads above VTL to reach pullout are optional; unload/reload cycles are rarely done. Table 9.1: AL for 1 min; 0.13, 0.25, 0.38, 0.50 and 0.63 VTL held 10 min (read at 1, 2, 4, 5, 10); 0.75 VTL creep test held 60 min (read at 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 20, 30, 50, 60); 0.88 and 1.00 VTL 10 min; AL 1 min with permanent movement recorded; AL commonly <= 0.025 VTL. Optional stepped unloading, one to seven steps held until gauges are stable, defines the unloading curve and separates elastic and non-recoverable movement. Acceptance: pullout does not occur below 1.00 VTL; the total movement at VTL exceeds 80 percent of the theoretical elastic elongation of the unbonded length, Delta_VTL > 0.8 VTL LUB / (E At) with E = 29,000 ksi (Eq. 9.4), which ensures load transfer only in the bonded length; creep within Section 9.4.5. Specifications are in Appendices E and F; Figure 9.4 is a model data sheet and Figure 9.5 an example of elastic movement data reduction.
key_points: Sacrificial nails built as designed and by production methods; ideally to pullout, at least to the nominal bond strength
Unbonded length at least 3 ft in the hole, plus jack and tail length; no fully grouted test nails
Eq. 9.1 LB VT max = At fy CRTY / rPO (CRTY 0.9, ASTM A615); Eq. 9.2 = At fu CRTU / rPO (CRTU 0.8, ASTM A722)
10 ft <= LB VT <= LB VT max; if LB VT max < 10 ft, use 10 ft and a larger tendon
Eq. 9.3 VTL = LB VT rPO: an ultimate load with no pullout safety or resistance factor
Table 9.1: increments of 0.13 VTL held 10 min; creep test at 0.75 VTL for 60 min; AL <= 0.025 VTL
Acceptance: no pullout below 1.00 VTL; Delta_VTL > 0.8 VTL LUB/(E At), E = 29,000 ksi (Eq. 9.4); creep per 9.4.5
Optional stepped unloading (one to seven steps) separates elastic and permanent movement

subsections.title: Details of Proof Tests
subsections.summary: Proof tests are single-cycle tests to the proof test load PTL; temporary unbonded length at least 3 ft in the hole plus jack and tail length. LB PT max = At fy CRTY / (rPO x 0.75) (Eq. 9.5) or At fu CRTU / (rPO x 0.75) (Eq. 9.6); the bond length is 10 ft or LB PT max, whichever is smaller; nails shorter than 12 ft may use less; fully grouted nails are not proof tested. PTL = LB PT rPO 0.75 (Eq. 9.7). Table 9.2: increments of 0.17 PTL until stable, creep at 1.0 PTL for 10 min (60 if over 0.04 in.). Acceptance: no pullout below 1.0 PTL; movement over 0.8 PTL LUB/(E At) (Eq. 9.8); creep per 9.4.5.
subsections.body: 9.4.4 Details of Proof Tests (pp. 253-255). Proof tests are single-cycle tests with load applied in increments to a maximum proof test load (PTL). Proof test nails also have a bonded length and a temporary unbonded length from the back of the bearing plate to the top of the grouted length, at least 3 ft within the hole, with extra bar outside (jack length and 'tail' length) for the test assembly. The bonded length LB PT is chosen so a bond limit is reached before a tensile limit state: (1) LB PT max = At x fy x CRTY / (rPO x 0.75) for Grade 75 and other mild steel per ASTM A615 (as printed; the caption of Eq. 9.5 reads Grades 60 and 75), or At x fu x CRTU / (rPO x 0.75) for Grade 150 and other high-strength steel per ASTM A722 (Eq. 9.6); (2) select LB PT max (as printed) to be 10 ft or LB PT max, whichever is smaller, to avoid tensile breakage. Production proof test nails shorter than 12 ft may be tested with less than the minimum 10-ft bond length; fully grouted test nails must not be proof tested. The maximum proof load is PTL = LB PT x rPO x 0.75 (Eq. 9.7), a maximum load, not a multiple of a 'design' load, so the Table 9.2 schedule differs from the previous manual. Each increment is held at least 10 minutes with movements recorded at each increment and the tabulated times; creep tests are at 1.00 PTL. Table 9.2: AL for 1 min (AL <= 0.025 PTL); 0.17, 0.33, 0.50, 0.67 and 0.83 PTL held until movement stabilizes (in creep-susceptible soils, 10 minutes with readings at 1, 2, 5 and 10); 1.0 PTL creep test held 10 min, read at 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 10; if the movement between 1 and 10 minutes exceeds 0.04 in., PTL is held 50 more minutes with readings at 20, 30, 50 and 60, and the permanent movement recorded; AL 1 min. Times are measured after each target load is reached. Acceptance: no pullout below 1.0 PTL; total movement at PTL greater than 80 percent of the theoretical elastic elongation of the unbonded length, Delta_PTL > 0.8 PTL LUB / (E At) (Eq. 9.8); creep within Section 9.4.5.

Eq. 9.5 LB PT max = At fy CRTY / (rPO x 0.75); Eq. 9.6 = At fu CRTU / (rPO x 0.75)

subsections.title: Details of Creep Tests
subsections.summary: Creep tests, part of verification and proof tests, hold a constant load and plot deflection against log time. Verification: creep under 0.04 in. between 1 and 10 minutes and under 0.08 in. between 6 and 60 minutes at 0.75 VTL, with a linear or decreasing rate. Proof: under 0.04 in. between 1 and 10 minutes; if exceeded, PTL held 50 more minutes and creep under 0.08 in. between 6 and 60 minutes. Criteria come from ground anchor practice (Figure 9.6).
subsections.body: 9.4.5 Details of Creep Tests (pp. 255-257). Creep tests, part of verification and proof tests, are conducted at a specified constant test load with displacements recorded at specified intervals; deflection against log-time is plotted on a semi-log graph and compared with the specification's acceptance criteria. Verification tests: creep movement between the 1- and 10-minute readings at 0.75 VTL less than 0.04 in.; between the 6- and 60-minute readings at 0.75 VTL less than 0.08 in.; and a creep rate linear or decreasing throughout the hold. Proof tests: creep movement less than 0.04 in. between the 1- and 10-minute readings; if exceeded, PTL is maintained 50 more minutes with readings at 20, 30, 50 and 60 minutes; if extended, the movement between the 6- and 60-minute readings is less than 0.08 in. The criteria are based on experience and current practice with ground anchors, to ensure design loads are carried safely through the service life. Figure 9.6 shows an example of data reduction for the creep movement between the 1- and 10-minute readings.
key_points: Deflection plotted against log time at constant load
Verification: less than 0.04 in. (1-10 min) and 0.08 in. (6-60 min) at 0.75 VTL; linear or decreasing rate
Proof: less than 0.04 in. (1-10 min); else hold 50 more minutes and less than 0.08 in. (6-60 min)
Criteria from ground anchor experience

subsections.title: Strain Gauges
subsections.summary: Strain gauges measure tendon axial strain, giving load from the steel modulus (typically 29,000 ksi); several spot-weldable gauges along the tendon give the load distribution and mobilized bond between gauges, load changes over time, and bond in tests without pullout or across strata. Disregarding cracked grout can overestimate mobilized bond at low loads; account for the grout modulus below its limit tensile strain. Install redundant gauges where readings are critical.
subsections.body: 9.4.6 Strain Gauges (pp. 257-258). Strain gauges can measure the axial strain of the tendon during testing; with the steel modulus (typically 29,000 ksi) the axial load at the gauge can be calculated. Several spot-weldable gauges along the tendon give the variation of axial load along the nail, so the change in load and the average mobilized bond between consecutive gauges can be estimated under any load, the load increase over time assessed, and often the full mobilization of bond along a portion of the tendon identified before pullout. The grout is typically assumed cracked in tension and its strength and stiffness disregarded, which may cause significant errors in the interpreted load at low loads and overestimate the mobilized bond; the grout modulus should generally be accounted for if the measured strain is less than the limit tensile strain of the grout. Strain gauges allow the actual bond resistance to be determined in tests without pullout, and variations of bond in nails bonded in two or more strata. Where correct readings are critical, redundant gauges must be installed.
key_points: Axial load from tendon strain and the steel modulus (typically 29,000 ksi)
Gauges along the tendon give the load distribution and mobilized bond between gauges
Account for the grout modulus when strain is below its limit tensile strain
Bond resistance without pullout and across strata; redundant gauges where critical

sections.title: Instrumentation and Monitoring
sections.summary: Instrumentation and monitoring: when to monitor (9.5.1), the parameters monitored (9.5.2), the monitoring and action plan (9.5.3) and the instruments: inclinometers, survey points, strain gauges and nail head load cells (9.5.4).
sections.body: 9.5 Instrumentation and Monitoring (pp. 258-263). Subsections 9.5.1 Introduction to 9.5.4 Monitoring Instruments.
key_points: Deformation monitoring with inclinometers and survey points; strain gauges and load cells for nail loads
sections.applicability: Performance monitoring plans, action plans and instruments for soil nail walls.

subsections.title: Introduction
subsections.summary: Performance monitoring should be included in any critical or unusual installation (road widening under existing bridges, high surcharges) and considered when an Owner builds its first permanent soil nail wall: inclinometers, top-of-wall survey points, load cells and strain gauges, monitored for at least 1 year after construction to cover load, time and seasonal (freeze-thaw) effects.
subsections.body: 9.5.1 Introduction (p. 258). Performance monitoring should be included in any critical or unusual soil nail wall installation, such as walls for road widening under existing bridges and walls with high surcharge loading, and should be considered when a permanent soil nail wall is constructed by an Owner for the first time. Instrumentation for such walls should include inclinometers, top-of-wall survey points, load cells and strain gauges: inclinometers and survey points measure wall movements during and after construction, and strain gauges in individual nails measure the development and distribution of nail forces to improve future designs. Monitoring for at least 1 year after construction is recommended, to examine service deformation and stress development in the nails and facing as functions of load, time and environmental changes such as winter freeze-thaw cycles.
key_points: Monitoring for critical or unusual walls (under existing bridges, high surcharges) and an Owner's first permanent wall
Inclinometers, top-of-wall survey points, load cells and strain gauges
Monitor at least 1 year after construction
subsections.applicability: When to instrument and monitor soil nail walls.

subsections.title: Monitored Parameters
subsections.summary: Deformation of the wall or slope during and after construction is the most significant indicator of overall performance. Inclinometers along and at distances behind the face give the most comprehensive ground deformation data at their sections; optical survey points at the top of the wall and, where practical, on the face give face deformations to correlate with them.
subsections.body: 9.5.2 Monitored Parameters (pp. 258-259). The most significant indicator of overall performance of the soil nail wall system is the amount of deformation of the wall or slope during and after construction. Inclinometers along the face and at various distances from it provide the most comprehensive data on ground deformations at the sections where they are installed. Optical survey points at the top of the wall and, where practical, on the wall face provide actual face deformations that can be correlated with the inclinometer data at specific sections.
key_points: Wall or slope deformation is the main performance indicator
Inclinometers give the most comprehensive deformation data; survey points give face movement
subsections.applicability: Parameters monitored on soil nail walls.

subsections.title: Monitoring and Action Plan
subsections.summary: A minimum plan measures face movement (survey markers; inclinometers 3 to 8 ft behind the facing, not beyond 30 percent of the wall height for one row), top-of-wall and ground movement, ground cracks (daily inspection, crack gauges), facing deterioration and drainage. A comprehensive plan may add toe monitoring over fine-grained soils, paired strain gauges at 5-ft spacing and inclinometer arrays (Figure 9.7). The plan defines instruments, frequencies, reporting and parties, with movement thresholds and a Contractor action plan.
subsections.body: 9.5.3 Monitoring and Action Plan (pp. 259-261). Monitoring during construction gives data on overall wall performance. At a minimum, a plan typically measures: horizontal movements of the face with surface markers and optical surveying, and inclinometer casings 3 to 8 ft behind the facing, but generally not farther than 30 percent of the wall height if only one row is used; vertical and horizontal movements of the top of the facing and the ground behind it by optical survey; ground cracks and disturbance behind the top of the wall by daily visual inspection and, if necessary, crack gauges; local movement or deterioration of the facing by visual inspection and crack gauges; and drainage behavior, especially if groundwater is seen, by observation of outflow points or standpipe piezometers behind the facing. A more comprehensive plan (printed 'A more comprehensive monitoring plan soil nail wall performance- may be established') may be set for several reasons: over fine-grained soils, the ground at the toe and in front of the wall may be watched for cracking and bulging suggesting basal heave or global instability; walls stabilizing moving soils may need more instruments; and monitoring may check safety during construction, validate design changes or value engineering, control excavation rates, and build knowledge for future designs. It might include strain gauges along the nail for the magnitude and location of the maximum load and load redistribution in creep-susceptible soils, ideally in diametrically opposed pairs at 5-ft spacing with the tendon end inscribed to verify orientation, and inclinometer arrays at various distances behind the wall (typical layout, Figure 9.7). The monitoring program must be well defined in the design documents: instrument types and locations, frequency of measurements, observations and reporting, minimum reporting requirements, reporting lines and parties. Movement threshold criteria and an action plan are essential; the action plan, typically developed by the Contractor with minimum requirements possibly in the specifications, sets response steps for reasonably anticipated occurrences that can be carried out within the project and a reasonable time.
key_points: Minimum: face movement by survey markers and inclinometers 3 to 8 ft behind the facing (not beyond 30 percent of H for one row)
Minimum: top-of-wall and ground movement, ground cracks (daily), facing deterioration, drainage
Over fine-grained soils, watch the toe for cracking or bulging (basal heave, global instability)
Comprehensive: paired strain gauges at 5-ft spacing; inclinometer arrays (Figure 9.7)
Design documents define instruments, frequencies, reporting and parties
Movement thresholds and an action plan (typically by the Contractor) are essential
subsections.applicability: Monitoring and action plans for soil nail walls.

subsections.title: Monitoring Instruments
subsections.summary: Instruments are chosen for the parameter, reliability, simplicity and readout compatibility. Inclinometers give the most comprehensive deformation data; in-place types read rapidly but are checked periodically with a manual probe. Survey prisms read optically or by EDM to 0.1 in. or better within 300 ft; automated total stations reduce errors and separate seasonal from gravity movements. Vibrating wire strain gauges on sister bars (Figure 9.8) or spot-welded are most common. Head load cells show facing loads but occasionally read inaccurately.
subsections.body: 9.5.4 Monitoring Instruments (pp. 261-263). Instruments should be selected on the parameters to be measured, reliability and simplicity, and compatibility with the specified readout devices. Inclinometers (9.5.4a, p. 261) provide the most comprehensive data on wall deformations and are well-established and commercially available; in-place inclinometers, used extensively in recent years, allow rapid readings through the full depth without moving a probe, but should be verified with manual readings using a standard probe with certain frequency. Survey Points (9.5.4b, p. 261): reflector prisms on the wall face or on stable ground bases are read by optical surveying or electronic distance measuring (EDM) equipment; optical or laser systems typically measure horizontal and vertical displacements to 0.1 in. or better within a 300-ft range. Automated total stations, increasingly used, reduce reading errors with a semi-permanent instrument, read often enough to separate periodic environmental movements from gravity-induced ones, and may save cost on long projects. Strain Gauges (9.5.4c, p. 262) show nail load distribution as excavation proceeds and after completion. Vibrating wire strain gauges are the most common in U.S. soil nail testing, used with 'sister bars' (rebar pieces at each end, Figure 9.8) attached to the tendon before installation and grouting; the gauge frequency reading is converted by the datalogger to microstrain (strain = microstrain x 10^-6). Spot-weldable vibrating wire gauges may be used instead, and optical grating/fiber and resistance gauges also. Load Cells at the Nail Head (9.5.4d, p. 263) show the loads developed at the facing and their variation over time, but are known occasionally to read inaccurately; they typically use Wheatstone-resistance bridges on an element of known modulus, with vibrating wire and other types also available.
key_points: Select instruments by parameter, reliability, simplicity and readout compatibility
Inclinometers most comprehensive; in-place types checked with a manual probe periodically
Survey prisms by optical or EDM methods: 0.1 in. or better within 300 ft
Automated total stations reduce reading errors and separate environmental from gravity movements
Vibrating wire strain gauges with sister bars (Figure 9.8) most common in the U.S.; strain = microstrain x 10^-6
Nail head load cells occasionally read inaccurately
